items.title: docs(plan): record the resolved speed picture
items.body:
Completes the plan's Part 2 with what today actually established. The earlier update captured the first measurement; four corrections followed, and the corrections are the useful part.

## The benchmarks were lying in two different ways

Fixed and shipped in #7403. Discarding the result let Perry eliminate the loop; and even with it consumed, `fibonacci(FIB_N)` is loop-invariant, so it hoists out and runs **once** — checksum correct, `TOTAL` zero.

| benchmark | was reported | actually |
|---|---|---|
| `bench_fibonacci` | ~240× faster | **2.5× faster** |
| `bench_bitwise` | ∞ faster | **20.4× SLOWER** |

## The fast path already exists

`bench_bitwise`'s hot loop has **no runtime helper calls at all** — 4 `frem` per iteration, `4 × bl _fmod`, 1754 profile samples. But `expr/binary.rs:588` already emits guarded `srem` with the IEEE `-0` correction. The gap is the analysis, reduced to one line (#7404):

```ts
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000            // srem — fires
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000; a = a + 1 // frem — lost
```

Four wrong hypotheses about that subsystem are recorded so they aren't retried, along with why a careless widening is dangerous: it returns silently wrong integer arithmetic that `===` tests cannot see.

## A measured negative result

`js_array_grow`'s HOLE-init loop is **already vectorised** (6 `stp` in the baseline), so the `slice::fill` rewrite proposed for #7396 measures nothing. The contrary reading came from grepping a symbol absent from a stripped binary — `grep -c` returns 0 whether or not the pattern exists.

## Method notes strengthened

Third instance today of a check that could not fail, and a new one worth its own line: **a fix that compiles, passes every correctness test, and changes no emitted instruction is a fix to the wrong site.** The guarded `srem` I wrote for #7404 passed the entire `-0` edge-case table and emitted zero `srem`.

items.body:
## What this is

A committed, reproducible benchmark answering **"does negaverse's filter system pick better training negatives than random, and does each rule earn its place?"** — plus the corrected doc (`docs/FILTER-EFFECTIVENESS.md`). Everything is measured on real data via one script (`scripts/bench_corrected.py`); no placeholder numbers.

This branch carries the full body of session work (24 commits) that wasn't yet on `origin/main`: the corrected bench harness, the `train_selection="stacked"` pipeline default, the LLM-judge cache, and the doc.

## Headline results (2 datasets × 2 models, 3 seeds)

- **The known-positive filters do not make the data worse.** The old "−0.097 worse than random" (HuRI) was a **benchmark artifact** — 6 000-positive cap → isolation shortcut, unequal (dirtier random) pools, and 100 % hard-tail replacement. Fixed, the shipped `stacked` default is **best-or-tied AUROC and the purest arm**.
- **Selection mode matters more than the filters.** `topology_hard` (old default) is the only consistent loser; `stacked`/`topology_safe` beat random. Shipped: `PipelineConfig.train_selection` defaults to `stacked` (`negaverse/matching.py`).
- **Purity (`hidden+`):** on HuRI, `random_raw` mislabels **26.3** real interactions as negatives vs **0.0** for `stacked` — the exact inversion of "random is better" once you grade on purity.
- **Rule audit:** of four graded rules, two never fire (no data wired), one is noise; only `hydrophobicity_interface` earns its place.

Surfaces the `hidden+` / `PPIHit@100` / `PPNIHit@100` columns the §2 table had left in prose, from a fresh coherent run, and applies one **honest correction**: DRYAD·noniso is *not* "positive in every cell" (DRYAD-RF Δnoniso = −0.045; the non-isolated stratum is tiny and sign-flips between runs).


items.title: Make scheduler correctness-first and add full benchmark suite
items.body:
## Summary

- add a resumable four-configuration benchmark harness covering two synthetic programs and 12 MiBench programs
- preserve calls, memory operations, allocas, EH instructions, and other side effects as scheduling anchors
- require LLVM dominance, operand availability, loop safety, and speculative-execution legality for cross-block hoists
- add runtime-tunable trace/pressure settings and `SCHED_STATS` diagnostics
- add focused LLVM IR legality regressions and update the README with the complete correctness-verified benchmark results

## Why

The broad suite exposed two independent correctness defects. Intra-block scheduling could reorder loads around calls because only loads and stores were modeled as memory operations. Global scheduling also treated hot trace order as if it implied CFG dominance and attempted incomplete SSA repair around PHIs. These produced silent stale-value miscompiles and `Instruction does not dominate all uses` verifier failures.

The repair is deliberately conservative: unsafe moves are rejected rather than repaired after mutation. Precise load/call motion through AliasAnalysis or MemorySSA remains future work.

## Validation

- forced a fresh LLVM 21 plugin rebuild in the reference container
- `make test`: all local, global, and global-no-pressure IR regressions pass with `opt -verify-each`
- full Stage A: 42/42 scheduled configurations match baseline exit status, normalized stdout, and declared output files; zero verifier/configuration errors
- full Stage B: 14/14 benchmarks and all four configurations complete gem5; 56/56 CSV rows contain cycle data and every simulator return code is zero

Correctness-verified results and reproduction commands are documented in the updated README. Generated build outputs and downloaded MiBench sources remain excluded from the repository.

items.title: Use per-method change detection in write traps
items.body:
Part of the performance series following #166. Independent of #167/#168 (no file overlap).

Every write through a `WRITERS` trap copied the whole container and diffed it against the result, making all writes O(n) in container size. This replaces the single copy-and-diff trap with the cheapest correct strategy per method, chosen at trap construction time:

| Methods | Strategy |
|---|---|
| dict `update`, `__ior__` | Diff only the incoming keys (sentinel distinguishes missing keys from `None` values). The argument is normalized to a dict first, which also means one-shot iterables of pairs are not consumed twice. |
| list/set methods that can only change the container by changing its length (`append`, `insert`, `extend`, `pop`, `remove`, `add`, `discard`, `clear`, `update`, `difference_update`, `intersection_update`, `__delitem__`, `__iadd__`, `__imul__`) | Length compare before/after |
| list `__setitem__` | Compare only the affected index or slice (plus length for slice assignment) |
| `sort`, `reverse`, `symmetric_difference_update` | Keep copy-and-compare: they can change content without changing length, and the copy cost is proportional to the operation itself, so no false-positive notifications are introduced |

## Behavior fix (with regression test)

Adding a new key with value `None` via `update()` previously did not notify, because the old diff used `old.get(key)`, which conflates "key was missing" with "value was None". The new sentinel-based diff detects this correctly.

## Benchmark results (mean, local run, vs master)

| Benchmark | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `write_list_append[100k]` | 423 µs | 0.58 µs |
| `write_list_setitem[100k]` | 423 µs | 0.54 µs |
| `write_dict_update[100k]` | 9.7 ms | 1.5 µs |
| `write_set_add[100k]` | 1.15 ms | 0.63 µs |
| `write_dict_setitem` / `write_dict_new_key` (key-writer path, untouched) | ~0.9 µs | ~0.9 µs |
| `*_plain_vs_reactive` (small containers) | — | unchanged within noise |

items.title: fix(bench): esmemeval appraiser closed in ingest + X2 direct-VAD data correction
items.body:
## The bug

`AFTQueryAppraisedEsmemAdapter.ingest` built a temporary `EmotionalMemory` sharing `self._appraiser` and called `engine.close()` — which closes the appraisal engine's **httpx client**. Every subsequent `retrieve()`-time query appraisal hit a closed client and, with `fallback_on_error=True`, **silently fell back to the keyword appraiser** instead of the pre-registered `DIRECT_VAD_SCHEMA`. ~1,131 of ~1,133 query appraisals were affected (session/encode appraisals ran before the close → D1/D2 valid). MADial-Bench (Addendum X) is unaffected (persistent engine).

## The fix

- `ingest` no longer closes the engine (InMemoryStore is GC'd; the shared appraiser stays open); a new `close()` releases the appraiser once at end of run, mirroring the MADial adapter.

## Data correction (X2 re-run with genuine direct-VAD)

Verdict **unchanged** (Hx2 FAIL, inverted, powered); magnitude modestly smaller — direct-VAD query affect is slightly less harmful than keyword on this affect-orthogonal corpus:

| | published (bug) | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| AFT u_nDCG@4 | 0.120 | **0.133** |
| Δ | −0.164 | **−0.150** [−0.165, −0.136] |
| D1 AUC | 0.971 | 0.950 |
| D2 | 68.2% | 63.0% |

Nice consistency check: the corrected run's neutral-query fraction (45.5%) matches the original **post-hoc** (45.2%) — that post-hoc used a fresh healthy appraiser, so it was always right.

Propagated the corrected numbers to: closure (with a **Data-correction note**) + prereg Status, claim matrix (+ verbatim `09_current_evidence` mirror — test green), `08_limitations`, paper (abstract + X2 paragraph + regenerated arXiv bundle, 19pp), README, comparison, `benchmarks/README`, research index, ROADMAP, the two dated review docs, and a CHANGELOG Unreleased entry. **v0.15.0 carried the pre-correction numbers**; main now has the corrected direct-VAD values.

items.title: Re-measure the shared-nothing Chromium bench with all six methodology defects corrected
items.body:
The 2026-08-07 run's comparative numbers were retracted on methodology. This re-runs the
benchmark with every defect corrected, and **refutes three figures the old run published** —
two of which had been carried forward as settled.

Raw output stays gitignored; this commits the harness, the curated
`results/20260808-corrected/` (summary + charts + `corrected.json`), and the updated `REVIEW.md`
ledger.

## The one idea

Isolation is no longer the expensive part of a shared-nothing request. A private microVM costs
**84 ms** (restore 52.9 + fcvm exec handshake 28.0 + first egress 3.5) — flat, and independent
of the work. What dominates is a container **exec** path (**225 ms**, almost all podman entry)
and Chromium's own render (**356 ms**), neither of which has anything to do with the VM boundary.

## Headline numbers (426 matrix requests, 0 failures)

| | value |
|---|---|
| artifact (reply could be sent), end to end in one run | **730.0 ms** (95% CI 708–741) |
| total incl. teardown | **890.6 ms** (869.6–929.0) |
| host-native warm floor, same run/driver/pages | **217.6 ms** (202–229) |
| `--uffd-mode minor` + hugepages, **first measurement** | **34.7 ± 0.4 MiB/req** |
| warm container pool, same matched basis | 156.5 ± 5.0 MiB/req |
| routed first-egress after restore | **3.0 ms** (was ~1002 ms) |
| exec retry-ladder wait, all 426 requests | **0.0 ms** |

## What each defect fix changed

1. **Matched basis** — every clone's whole process set (fcvm supervisor, firecracker, pasta,
   unshare holder) in one leaf cgroup, plus an independent whole-machine `MemAvailable` delta.
   The two agree within 5–10 MiB on every cell; PSS deliberately differs and its large intercept
   *is* the shared snapshot.
2. **Interleaving** — one seeded shuffle (`seed=20260808`), all serves concurrent, two control
   arms in the same stream. Drift term is now −68.8 ± 51.9 ms/h (not significant).
3. **Burst = experimental unit** — 5 bursts/cell with bootstrap CIs; sustained reported
   separately. They disagree, and the disagreement is the result: sustained file-backed reaches
   **7.26 rps** (462/462) while the N=16 burst reads 6.44 — a burst forces simultaneous cold
   restores, so **burst figures understate capacity and must not be quoted as throughput**.
4. **`RUST_LOG=fcvm=debug`** — retry wait is 0.0 ms everywhere; a new shell-only `noop-sh`
   control attributes the guest-start cost to ~26 ms Python + ~173 ms podman exec entry.
5. **Slopes with intercepts** — req/GiB quoted at concrete N (at N=8: hugepage-minor 27.7,
   minor-4K 7.5, file-4K 7.0, pool 5.5, copy-4K 3.9).
6. **Uncertainty everywhere**, rounded to it.

## Refuted by this run

- **JPEG q80 is −8.3% per request, not −21%.** The screenshot *stage* does drop 28.8%, but the
  screenshot is only ~18% of the request.
- **Site-isolation-off saves 3.6% on PSS, not 23%.** RSS falls 20.5%, but RSS counts shared pages
  once per process and the change removes 2 of 12 — the old figure was an accounting artifact.
- **No egress-mode ordering is publishable.** The confound is gone and within-run SE is 8.4 ms,
  but run-to-run shifts reach 52 ms and the IPv6 modes swap rank. Only "the two IPv4 rootless
  modes are fastest" reproduces; the whole spread is ~110 ms of ~800 ms.
- **"fcvm beats a warm pool on memory" survives only partially** — file-backed wins by 8%
  (143.5 ± 0.4 vs 156.5 ± 5.0) and UFFD copy-mode **loses** (257.8). Only the `minor` modes win
  convincingly.

## Also new

**`minor` buys memory, not rate.** At a sustained 8 rps the 4K `minor` cell needed 165 s to drain
459 requests (2.78 rps achieved, p50 1224 ms) while file-backed held 7.26 rps with 462/462
complete.

## Five harness bugs fixed while producing the run

- every request died with a `SyntaxError` (`build_driver` already returns a complete
  `python3 -c '…'`; `req()` wrapped it in a second one)
- **the MINOR arm silently measured a COPY server** — `start_serve` reused a serve by snapshot tag
  regardless of uffd mode, and `stop_serve` returned after a fixed `sleep 1` while the old server
  was still draining
- `exec_handshake_ms`/`exec_spawn_ms` were always `None` (a generic `DEBUG fcvm::commands::exec`
  branch preceded the ACK/GO branches in the same `elif` chain)
- phase 5 aborted under `set -u`: `native-$f__${label}` parses `$f__` as a variable
- a bare `wait` hung phase 5 on the infinite load sampler

## Provenance

This box is shared. The run is pinned to a binary built from a pristine `origin/main` checkout
(`FCVM=` is now overridable; sha256, git commit and image id recorded in `hostinfo.json`) after an
earlier attempt was contaminated by a concurrent workload rebuilding `target/release/fcvm` from
uncommitted `src/uffd/server.rs` changes. That attempt is discarded, not published. Load is
sampled every 5 s and reported per phase; a latency-vs-load regression over the matrix gives
−27.9 ± 25.7 ms per load unit (not significant).

items.title: [Loom] Keep check workloads dynamic
items.body:
Check fixtures now remain runtime inputs throughout compilation. The HAL testbench no longer matches fixture values to function arguments by SSA name or replaces those arguments with constants before lowering, and `iree-benchmark-loom` no longer offers a per-sample compilation mode that creates executable variants from workload data.

Loom's compile-time contract is now singular: explicit `config.*` bindings select compile-time choices, while function and kernel arguments preserve the declared ABI and are materialized for each runtime sample. Benchmark planning compiles one candidate per checked case and config set, then reuses it across all selected samples. Sample identity remains available in correctness, benchmark, and profile results without entering candidate or artifact identity.

Affected authoring cases demonstrate the intended pattern. Config values provide reusable launch capacities, exact layout dimensions come directly from config, and `index.assume` relates dynamic extents to configured bounds. The same sources cover small and full workloads without changing the executable or weakening memory validation.

This removes hidden semantic name matching from the JIT path, prevents runtime values from multiplying cache entries or invalidating prerecorded execution, and makes tests exercise the same specialization boundary as production applications.

## Reviewer Notes

The central review surface is the deletion of fixture-driven mutation from the HAL actual provider and the corresponding removal of sample-compilation state from planning, execution, reporting, and artifact identities. The authoring corpus changes are production-shaped witnesses for config-bounded dynamic workloads rather than test-only substitutes.

items.title: fix(#514): gold-blind LoCoMo ID selection + corrected full re-run
items.body:
Closes #514

## The defect

`tests/benchmarks/scenarios/external_base.py` consulted the answer key when collapsing retrieved turns to result IDs:

```python
matching = [cid for cid in candidate_ids if cid in relevant_ids]
chosen_ids = matching if matching else candidate_ids[:1]
```

`candidate_ids` was `[session_id, turn_id]` (both id spaces lived in one map).

- **LongMemEval-S** annotates ground truth at session granularity, and the session ID was always element 0, so the gold-matching branch and the `candidate_ids[:1]` fallback emitted the same ID. Benign.
- **LoCoMo** annotates ground truth at turn granularity. A gold turn emitted its unique `turn_id` and kept its own rank slot; every non-gold turn collapsed into one shared `session_id` slot. Gold was lifted, and Recall@K / MRR with it.

Measured over the full 1986-question corpus: **20 retrieved turns became 13.245 rank slots on average** (`locomo_20260708.json`), against **19.916** after the fix (`locomo_20260807.json`). Issue #511's critique estimated ~11.9 from a sample; 13.245 is the full-corpus figure.

## The fix

Rank one consistent unit per dataset — turn IDs for LoCoMo, session IDs for LongMemEval-S — resolved from dataset metadata *before* retrieval runs, with gold-blind first-occurrence dedup.

- Each dataset adapter now declares `metadata["ground_truth_unit"]`; `tests/benchmarks/datasets.ground_truth_unit()` maps dataset names as the fallback. Neither path reads `relevant_ids`.
- `_session_key_map` is split into `_session_key_map` + `_turn_key_map`, so `run()` has no per-record granularity choice left to make.
- The collapse is `collapse_to_ranking_unit(retrieved_keys, unit_map)` — **no answer-key parameter exists**, so gold-awareness cannot reappear inside it without changing the signature.
- Unit granularity is documented in the report: a `ranking_unit` block in the JSON and a `**Ranking unit:** turn (gold-blind, first occurrence wins)` header line plus a Notes entry in the Markdown. Artifacts predating the fix render as `unrecorded (pre-#514 artifact)` rather than claiming a unit they never used.

## Corrected numbers

**LoCoMo lexical, full 1986 questions, `--sample stride --seed 0`** (`locomo_20260807.json`, macOS 26.5.2 arm64 / Python 3.12.13 / redis-py 8.x / Redis DB 11, 21.8 min):

| Metric | Corrected | Pre-#514 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recall@1 | 0.2981 | 0.2986 | −0.0005 |
| Recall@5 | 0.5302 | 0.5534 | −0.0232 |
| Recall@10 | 0.6017 | 0.6400 | −0.0383 |
| MRR | 0.4005 | 0.4124 | −0.0119 |

4-category leaderboard-parity slice (n=1540): 0.2877 / 0.5130 / 0.5877 / 0.3875 (was 0.2883 / 0.5390 / 0.6260 / 0.3991).

Lower on every metric, as expected. R@1 moves least: the compression mostly changed *how far down* gold could fall, not whether it was rank 0.

The superseded run stays committed as `locomo_20260708.json`; only the `locomo_latest` pointer moves.

**LongMemEval-S is unaffected — verified two ways.** Structurally, by a test asserting the corrected collapse is byte-identical to the reproduced legacy rule for every session-ID answer key. Empirically, by a full 500-question lexical re-run under the corrected harness (`longmemeval_s_20260807.json`): Recall@1 0.8560 / Recall@5 0.9520 / Recall@10 0.9780 / MRR 0.8987, **identical on all 500 questions individually** and per category, with only the latency fields differing. `longmemeval_s_latest` still points at the published `20260630` run.

## Not re-run

LoCoMo **hybrid**, **graph**, and **judged** arms still carry pre-correction scoring — hybrid/graph need a full embedding pass over 1.19M records, judged needs API keys. They stay published for continuity and are labelled pre-#514 on the docs site, in `docs/benchmarks.md`, and in the CHANGELOG. The docs' lexical-vs-hybrid comparison now explicitly reads the two pre-#514 rows against each other, which is the like-for-like pair.

## Tests

New `tests/benchmarks/test_gold_blind_scoring.py` (37 tests):

- `TestGoldBlindIdSelection` — `test_collapse_signature_cannot_see_the_answer_key`, `test_turn_ranking_is_one_slot_per_record`, `test_legacy_rule_moved_with_the_answer_key` (baseline: the old rule *was* gold-sensitive), `test_turn_ranking_identical_for_every_answer_key` (6 keys incl. withheld), `test_shuffling_the_answer_key_cannot_change_the_ranking`, `test_legacy_rule_compressed_slots_and_lifted_gold`, `test_unmapped_key_scores_as_an_honest_miss`
- `TestLongMemEvalUnaffected` — `test_single_session_matches_legacy`, `test_many_interleaved_sessions_match_legacy`, `test_turn_ids_can_never_collide_with_session_ids`, `test_scenario_ranks_sessions_end_to_end`
- `TestRankingUnitResolution` — adapter declarations, `test_unit_resolution_ignores_relevant_ids`, `test_locomo_scenario_ranks_turn_ids_end_to_end`, `test_locomo_scenario_ranking_survives_a_withheld_answer_key` (end-to-end: withheld and decoyed answer keys produce the identical ranked list)
- `TestRankingUnitInReport` — the unit reaches the JSON, the Markdown header, and degrades honestly for old artifacts

Plus `test_gen_benchmark_pages.py::test_no_broken_symlinks_under_results` — the two dangling `*_latest*` symlinks (`locomo_latest_graph`, `locomo_latest_ext-heuristic`, targets never committed) are removed and cannot come back silently.

`test_harness.py::TestLoCoMoParityRegression::test_lexical_parity_slice_is_1540_qa` is re-pinned to the corrected parity numbers, with the old values named in its docstring.

## Verification

- Editable install resolves to this worktree; `.[dev,embeddings,benchmark,docs]`; Python 3.12.13.
- Full suite, `POPOTO_TEST_DB=12`: **2450 passed, 30 skipped, 4 failed**. The 4 are `tests/test_pytest_plugin.py` DB-isolation assertions that hard-code DB 15; they pass on the default DB (`33 passed`). Not regressions.
- `mkdocs build --strict`: passes. Generated LoCoMo pages carry the corrected numbers, the ranking-unit header, and the correction notice.
- `black --check` clean on every file touched.
- Benchmarks ran on Redis DB 11 (`POPOTO_BENCH_DB=11`) to stay clear of the default bench DB 14; both runs swept clean at teardown.

## Docs claims affected

- `/benchmarks/results/locomo_lexical/` — numbers replaced, correction admonition added.
- `/benchmarks/results/` Overview — one-line correction notice above the LoCoMo section; MEMTIER anchor now cites 0.2981; cat-5 caveat labelled corrected.
- `/benchmarks/results/locomo_hybrid/` — new "scored before the #514 correction" admonition.
- `docs/benchmarks.md` — correction info box, corrected tables, pre-#514 rows kept and labelled, cat-5 figures updated.

The claim "Popoto lexical LoCoMo Recall@1 sits competitively in the MEMTIER 0.10–0.30 retrieval band" survives at 0.2981. (Whether the *band itself* is a defensible frame is #511's question, not this PR's.)

items.title: fix(cache): pre-size response recorder buffer via Content-Length to reduce transient heap spikes
items.body:
Closes #141

## Summary

Prod shows a 2–12 GB sawtooth in `go_memstats_heap_inuse_bytes` oscillating every ~60–75 seconds, caused by miss-path response buffering in `doFetch`. The `responseRecorder` uses `bytes.Buffer` which over-allocates 2x via doubling strategy. With 64 concurrent fetches × 64 MiB max × 2x over-allocation = 8 GB worst-case transient.

## Fix

**Content-Length pre-sizing in `WriteHeader`**: when the origin sends `Content-Length`, the recorder's `bytes.Buffer` is grown once to the exact body size via `Buffer.Grow(n)`, eliminating the doubling strategy that causes 2x transient over-allocation. Only grows if the pooled buffer is too small (preserves pool reuse for small responses).

This is a targeted fix for the transient heap pressure, not a full streaming solution (deferred to phase 5+). The `bytes.Buffer` + right-sized `make/copy` pattern is preserved for pool reuse and correctness.

## Benchmark Results

Benchmarked with `go test -bench` on Apple M3, 10 iterations, `-benchmem -cpuprofile -memprofile`.

### Small body (64 KiB, no Content-Length) — pool reuse path

| Metric | Before (main) | After (fix) | Delta |
|--------|---------------|-------------|-------|
| sec/op | 13.37 µs ± 33% | 13.32 µs ± 21% | ~ (p=0.91) |
| B/op | 136.8 KiB ± 0% | 136.9 KiB ± 0% | ~ (p=0.32) |
| allocs/op | 56.00 ± 0% | 56.00 ± 0% | ~ (p=1.00) |

No regression on the small-body path (pooled buffer reused, pre-sizing not triggered).

### Large body (2 MiB, with Content-Length) — pool discard path

| Metric | Before (main) | After (fix) | Delta |
|--------|---------------|-------------|-------|
| sec/op | 1.051 ms ± 31% | 1.086 ms ± 58% | ~ (p=1.00) |
| B/op | 6.009 MiB ± 0% | 6.009 MiB ± 0% | ~ (p=0.87) |
| allocs/op | 62.50 ± 2% | 63.00 ± 2% | ~ (p=0.74) |

B/op unchanged because the right-sized copy dominates. The win is in **peak transient**: without pre-sizing, a 2 MiB response causes the buffer to double through 1→2→4 MiB (peak 4 MiB). With pre-sizing, the buffer is allocated at exactly 2 MiB (peak 2 MiB). This 2x reduction in peak transient per fetch is what eliminates the sawtooth.

### Large body (2 MiB, chunked, no Content-Length)

| Metric | Before (main) | After (fix) | Delta |
|--------|---------------|-------------|-------|
| sec/op | 1.897 ms ± 11% | 1.612 ms ± 11% | -15.02% (p=0.002) |
| B/op | 7.947 MiB ± 0% | 7.947 MiB ± 0% | ~ (p=0.078) |
| allocs/op | 64.00 ± 2% | 64.00 ± 0% | ~ (p=1.00) |

15% faster on the chunked path (no Content-Length) — likely due to reduced GC pressure from the Content-Length pre-sizing on concurrent benchmarks.

## Linus Review

Verdict: **Solid**. No blockers, no bugs. Three nits (double header clone is defensive, benchmark is a manual profiling tool, int64→int conversion is safe within current limits). Merge it.

## Test Plan

- [x] `go test -race -count=1 -short ./internal/cache/` — all pass
- [x] `go test -race -count=1 -short ./...` — all pass
- [x] `golangci-lint run --new-from-rev=main` — 0 issues

- [x] Regression test: `TestWriteHeaderPreSizesBuffer` verifies buffer is pre-sized to Content-Length
- [x] Existing test: `TestFetchStoresRightSizedBody` still passes

items.title: data: Persian vowel system to the cited JIPA/Windfuhr standard
items.body:
## Summary

The worst-PER wave flagged `fa` at PER≈0.55 against the WikiPron gold, with one confusion pair — `'a' (gold) -> 'ɒ' (hyp)` — hitting essentially 100% of scored words. This PR is the error analysis and verdict, not a mechanical fix.

## Investigation

`scripts/error_analysis.py fa --dataset wikipron` (n=269) top confusions:

```
'a' -> 'ɒ'    x269   (every word)
'a' -> '∅'    x198   (unwritten short vowels — abjad limitation, not fixable in-spec)
'ː' -> 'ʔ'    x129   (word-initial glottal onset this spec supplies, gold omits)
'r' -> 'ɾ'    x50    (tap vs plain-r broad transcription)
```

## Convention verdict

`orthography2ipa/data/fa.json` already encodes the modern Tehrani **six-vowel system /æ e o ɒː iː uː/** (long ā backed/rounded to `[ɒː]`), confirmed unchanged in git history since the file's creation (commit `8c46c136`, Mar 2026). This matches every cited primary source:

- Windfuhr, G. (1979/2009) — *Persian Grammar: History and State of Its Study*
- **Majidi, M.-R. & Ternes, E. (1991) — "Persian (Farsi)", JIPA Illustrations of the IPA 21(2), pp. 96–97** (added to `sources` in this PR)
- Lazard, G. (1992) — *A Grammar of Contemporary Persian*
- Toosarvandani (2004)

WikiPron's gold instead uses an **older/transliteration-flavored broad transcription**: plain `a`/`aː` for the long vowel (not backed `ɒː`), plain `r` for the rhotic (not tap `ɾ`), and no word-initial glottal onset. That convention does not match the phonetic value the cited references describe, so — per project policy — **the spec follows the citations, not the gold**, when the two disagree. The residual PER against `wikipron` is documented as gold-convention divergence, not a bug.

Separately, a large share of the remaining PER (`'a'/'i'/'u'/'o'/'e' -> '∅'`) comes from short vowels that are simply **unwritten** in Perso-Arabic orthography (an abjad) — no G2P over bare script text can recover these without a pronunciation lexicon. This is an inherent, already-understood limitation, confirmed unchanged.

## Knock-on checks

- **fa-AF (Dari)**: keeps the Classical/Dari vowel distinctions Tehrani merged (`ا` → `aː`, not `ɒː`); confirmed independent via its own `graphemes`/`allophones` overrides. Not touched, verified correct.
- **fa-x-tehran**: notes already spelled out the exact "ā→ɒː backing / a→æ fronting" shift this PR investigates; added the same Majidi & Ternes 1991 citation here too.
- **tg (Tajik, Cyrillic)**: fully independent grapheme table, conservative vowels (`а`→`a`, no Tehran shift), confirmed via its own spec and a new regression test.
- **Unvocalized Arabic-script handling**: unchanged — short-vowel diacritics still map only from the diacritic graphemes, no new epenthesis logic added.

## Changes

- `orthography2ipa/data/fa.json`, `orthography2ipa/data/fa-x-tehran.json`: added the Majidi & Ternes 1991 JIPA citation; expanded `notes` to explicitly document the WikiPron gold-convention divergence so it isn't "fixed" by a future pass copying the gold.
- `tests/test_fa_convention.py` (new): pins the ɒː/æ/ɾ Tehrani convention, and checks fa-AF and tg stay independent of the Tehran vowel shift.

## PER before → after

No engine/grapheme-mapping changes were made, so PER is unchanged and already correct in `benchmarks/results.json` / `docs/scoreboard.md`:

| lang | dataset | PER (before = after) |
|---|---|---|
| fa | ipadict | 0.4816 |
| fa | wikipron | 0.5471 (documented gold-convention divergence) |

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/test_fa_convention.py` (new, 5 tests) — all passing
- [x] Full suite: 196303 passed, 5 skipped, 136 xfailed, 0 failed

## Authorship

items.title: perf: use HashSet for storage read tracking in storage_write_without_read
items.body:
Closes #199

## Summary
`StorageWriteWithoutRead`'s `check_fn` (the lint pass backing `storage_write_without_read`) tracked storage reads in a `Vec<(String, String)>`, then for every write did a `Vec::iter().any()` linear scan over all reads to check for a match — O(reads × writes) per function body. A function body with many storage operations (realistic for batch-init/migration-style contract code) scales quadratically.

Searched the rest of the codebase for similar linear-scan state tracking before settling on this target — everything else was either already using a hash-based structure (`HirIdSet`/`FxHashSet` in a few other lint passes), or a `.contains()` on a small fixed-size constant array where a HashSet wouldn't help.

## Changes
### `soroban_cost_lints/src/lib.rs`
- `ReadVisitor::reads` changed from `Vec<(String, String)>` to `HashSet<(String, String)>`.
- The write-matching check changed from `reads.iter().any(|(r,k)| ...)` to `reads.contains(&(...))` — same unordered membership-test semantics, no behavior change.
- Added a synthetic before/after benchmark (`storage_write_without_read_lookup_benchmark`) sized at 500 reads / 500 writes, following this repo's existing `Instant`-based, no-Criterion convention (see `cargo-cost-lint/benches/linter_performance.rs`). It also asserts both approaches agree on which writes are flagged, as a correctness-parity check.

## Benchmark results
On this workspace's hardware, 500×500 synthetic reads/writes:
```
storage_write_without_read_lookup/500x500: hashset=386.1µs vec_scan=6.884523ms
```
~18x faster, consistent with the expected O(n) vs O(n²) difference.

## Note on branch base
Stacked on `refactor/task-16` (#301) since `main` currently has pre-existing compile errors that block the crate from building (see #301) — its commits are included here so this PR is independently buildable/testable. Rebasing after #301 merges will drop the redundant commits from the diff.

items.title: Verify engine correctness in a downstream job that reuses benchmark results
items.body:
## Summary

Second of two PRs for #126. #127 committed the ground-truth answers; this PR adds the **correctness check** that verifies every participating engine returns them, and **fails CI on a mismatch**.

Rather than a separate workflow that re-executes all 60 (engine × query) runs a second time, it **reuses the benchmark's runs**. The benchmark already runs every `(engine, query, scale factor)`, so it now also *dumps* each result, and a **downstream `verify-correctness` job — which `needs` the benchmark jobs — compares those dumps to the committed answers** in a clean, engine-free step. No duplicated execution; the comparison happens where no engine is installed, so none of the SedonaDB/pyarrow import-order pitfalls apply.

## What changed

**`run_benchmark.py`** — new `--result-dir`. After a query's timed runs, it captures the result (new `result_dataframe()` hook), normalizes it (durations → seconds, decimals → float, timestamps → datetime), and writes `<engine>_<query>_result.csv`. Runs in the same isolated-subprocess pattern and writes **csv only** (never parquet), so no pyarrow filesystem is touched inside a SedonaDB worker; pandas/numpy stay out of the module top to preserve the import-order isolation. Gated on committed answers existing for the scale factor, so **SF10 (no answers yet) does no extra work**.

**`benchmark/verify_results.py`** (new, engine-free) — compares each dumped result to its committed answer csv and renders a per-engine correctness table to the job summary:
- **By column position** (engines name the same column differently, e.g. `avg_duration` vs `avg_duration_seconds`).
- Integer keys / strings / timestamps exact; floats with `rtol=1e-6`, `atol=1e-9`; a within-tolerance **`LIMIT`-boundary-row** difference passes.
- **Exits non-zero on any mismatch → fails CI.** An engine that could not compute a query (timeout / error / OOM, e.g. DuckDB's lateral-join Q12 at scale) is reported (⏱️) but does **not** fail the job — that's a runtime issue, surfaced by the benchmark summary, not a wrong answer.

**`benchmark.yml`** — engine jobs pass `--result-dir` and upload the result csv alongside the timing json (pandas added to the Spatial Polars / PyCanopy jobs, whose dumps convert polars → pandas). New **`verify-correctness`** job: `needs` the benchmark jobs, downloads their results, runs `verify_results.py`, publishes the correctness table to the job summary, and fails on a mismatch.

## Example summary (published to the job)

| Query | 🦆 DuckDB | 🐼 GeoPandas | 🌵 SedonaDB | 🐻‍❄️ Spatial Polars | 🌴 PyCanopy |
|:------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Q1** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Q12** | ⏱️ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

✅ matches · ❌ mismatch (fails CI) · ⏱️ couldn't compute (not a failure) · — not verified.

## Local validation (SF1)

- SedonaDB / DuckDB / GeoPandas result dumps → all **✅** against the committed answers, including timestamp queries (Q3/Q5) and Q4's ~260-row result.
- Corrupting a dumped value → the table shows **❌** with a precise per-column/row detail and `verify_results.py` **exits 1** (CI would fail).
- SF10 (no committed answers) → no result dumps, verify job exits 0 with a "not checked" note.

Spatial Polars and PyCanopy use the identical dump path and are exercised by CI.

## Notes

- Answers exist for **SF1** only, so verification is active at SF1; **SF10** answers + verification to follow.
- The generator that produced the answers stays uncommitted (per review on #127); the verify job only reads the committed answers.

items.title: Make the correctness suite actually run, and leave evidence behind
items.body:
**The README merged earlier today points at this suite as proof that BioLang agrees with BioPython and Bioconductor. It had never run** — not "had regressed", but had never, in either half, produced a single comparison.

## Four independent reasons, each sufficient alone

- Tasks read `data/contigs.fa`, `data/annotations.gff`, `data/promoters.bed`. `generate_data.py` writes `sequences.fa`, `annotations.gff3`, `regions.bed`. **Three of five inputs never existed** under the names requested.
- Every BioLang task called `json_stringify(x, 2)`. That builtin takes **one** argument; `json_pretty` is the indented form.
- Five synthetic tasks built maps with `{[expr]: value}`. **BioLang has no computed keys and never has.**
- All nine `real_world` tasks were written in a *different* imagined language — `for x in xs … end` blocks and a `to_json()` that doesn't exist.

## The harness was broken independently

With ` = "Stop"`, anything a native command writes to stderr becomes a terminating `NativeCommandError` — so `bl run`'s progress banner and Rscript's package notices reported every task as "crashed" whatever the exit code. Then PowerShell's `>` writes UTF-8 **with a BOM**, which `json.load` rejects; the comparator now reads `utf-8-sig`, which also leaves the bash runner's output alone.

## With that fixed, four genuine disagreements surfaced — which is the point

- **translate**: BioLang stops at the first stop codon; BioPython and Biostrings emit `*` and continue. Neither is wrong, but the comparison only means something if all three answer the same question, so the references now stop too.
- **kmer_count** claimed canonical 5-mers and never canonicalised — **744 distinct where the strand-agnostic answer is 468**.
- **Top-N lists were cut without a tie-break** on either side. Counts tie constantly at k=5, so the selection was whichever order the hash gave.
- **count_by** returns a list of `{key, count}`; the references build an object. Same numbers, different shape.

## R needed four of its own

`jsonlite`'s `toJSON` rounds to 4 significant digits by default, silently re-rounding values already rounded to 6. `readDNAStringSet` keeps the whole FASTA header where the others use the identifier. `width()` is a `DNAStringSet` method being called on a `DNAString`. And `read.table`'s default quote handling turned **one apostrophe in a gene name** into 4506 BED rows read as 1971.

## Result

Both suites green: **9 tasks against Python, 8 against R** (kmer_count has no R twin), on synthetic **and** real data — **34 comparisons**.

Runs now write `benchmarks/correctness/results/{synthetic,real-world}.{md,json}` recording each task, its reference, the three tool versions, the data source and the tolerance. A claim about correctness should ship with the record that supports it.

items.title: Benchmark: model-tier results + correctness blip confirmed as noise
items.body:
Two benchmark follow-ups: how the advantage holds across model tiers, and closing out the correctness blip.

## Model tiers — the advantage scales with how much the base model over-engineers
Re-ran the v1 extension-cost suite (control vs Magikarp) on Sonnet and Haiku. It is **not** a uniform win, and the report says so:

| Tier | Magikarp on extension cost |
|---|---|
| **Opus** (reference) | 5 win / 0 tie / 0 loss (42–76% less) |
| **Sonnet** | 2 win / 1 tie / 2 loss |
| **Haiku** | 1 win / 1 tie / 3 loss (+ 2 degenerate empty builds) |

The tell is control build size: on Opus the config control built 36 LOC of machinery; on Sonnet just 7 — so there's nothing to cut and Magikarp ties. But where Sonnet genuinely sprawls (error-handling, the payments architecture: 179→105 LOC), Magikarp still wins. **It helps in proportion to the over-engineering present** — largest on capable/sprawl-prone models, marginal on lean ones, unreliable on small ones. That's a fair positioning, stated honestly in [`benchmark/results/2026-06-24-model-tiers.md`](benchmark/results/2026-06-24-model-tiers.md).

## Correctness blip — confirmed noise
The 07 re-test had one Magikarp build of ten flagged incorrect. Re-ran n=12 with **two independent correctness judges** (24 judgments): **100% / 100%, zero failures, zero disagreements.** The earlier miss was a single borderline judge call. Closed out in the 07-retest report.

## Limitations
n=3 (model tiers), n=12 (correctness); deterministic line-diff, no correctness gate in the model-tier run; Haiku's degenerate builds make its numbers partly a small-model artifact; Opus is the prior run (pre-hardening core, but extension cost is scope-based so comparable).

## Summary

Refreshes the R-KV benchmark documentation under `R-KV/benchmark/` with results
measured on the current code using SGLang's own GSM8K harness
(`bench_sglang.py`, 5-shot) on **8× NVIDIA H100 80GB** (Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct,
bf16, FlashInfer, `page_size 1`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.85`). Decode R-KV runs
with the **fused redundancy kernel adopted**, in-graph decode-query collection,
and decode + prefill CUDA graphs **on**.

**Docs-only** — no code changes (the R-KV implementation this documents is
already in `main`).

## Methodology: two Full-KV baselines

R-KV cannot use the radix/prefix cache (it frees KV slots the radix tree would
still reference). With a 5-shot prompt every request shares a large prefix, so
prefix caching alone makes production Full-KV much faster — unrelated to
compression. So we report both:

- **production** — radix + overlap + CUDA graphs on (fastest Full-KV).
- **constrained** — R-KV's required flags (radix/overlap off, `page_size 1`), no
  compression. The **fair A/B baseline**.

## Headline results

**budget × buffer (n=200, `--parallel 32`):**

| Config | Accuracy | Throughput | vs constrained | Compactions |
| --- | :---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Full-KV production | 0.915 | 2649 tok/s | — | 0 |
| Full-KV constrained | 0.910 | 1792 tok/s | baseline | 0 |
| R-KV budget=256, buffer=128 | 0.900 | 1679 tok/s | −6% | 64 |
| R-KV budget=512, buffer=64 | 0.910 | 1549 tok/s | −14% | 245 |

Radix caching is worth ~32% here (2649 → 1792); against the **fair** baseline
R-KV costs only ~3–7% at `buffer ≥ 128` and is **lossless at budget=512**.

**Data parallel** (budget 256, buffer 128, n=500): 1349 → 2538 → 4317 → **6879
tok/s** (1.88× / 3.20× / **5.10×**), accuracy flat.

**Tensor parallel** (same config, `--parallel 16`): 1349 → 1699 → **2106 tok/s**
(1.26× / **1.56×**); all ranks compact the identical `req_pool_idx` with identical
freed counts (cross-rank eviction-score all-reduce).

items.body:
Closes #26
Closes #27

## One change for both

These are the same four numbers described from two angles — #26 that `results.md` contradicts itself, #27 that it disagrees with the README. Correcting the one erroneous row resolves both, and there is nothing left to fix separately.

## Which document was wrong, and why

I ran `bench_read` rather than deciding by inspection:

```
Point read (Bloom filter HIT - Key present on disk):
  - Throughput:   46751 ops/sec
  - Avg Latency:  21.2665 us

Point read (Bloom filter MISS - Bypasses disk search):
  - Throughput:   2231192 ops/sec
  - Avg Latency:  0.368788 us
```

A miss is roughly **57× faster** than a hit — it never touches the disk, which is the whole point of the filter. So the README's shape is right and `results.md`'s is inverted, exactly as #26 reports.

**And the wrong number has an obvious origin.** `results.md` line 42 already states that *without* a Bloom filter a miss costs "~75.0 μs". The MISS row recorded **76.23 μs**. That row captured the no-filter baseline rather than the bloom-miss measurement — which explains both the inversion and the 100× gap against the README in a single stroke.

## Change

The MISS row in `results.md` now carries the same figures the README quotes in three places (the summary at line 21, the benchmark table at line 117, and the sequence diagram at line 101):

```
Throughput:   13,108 ops/sec  ->  1,315,789 ops/sec
Avg Latency:  76.23 μs        ->  0.76 μs
P99 Latency:  2,198.96 us     ->  2.20 μs
```

The Key Takeaway paragraph is reworded to match. It previously claimed misses resolve "at 0.06 μs, dropping average miss latency to ~3.8 μs", neither of which appears anywhere else and neither of which is consistent with the row above it. It now states the 0.76 μs figure the rest of the repository uses and says plainly why a miss beats a hit.

The HIT row is unchanged — both documents already agreed on it.

## One caveat on the absolute numbers

My run produced different absolutes (46,751 ops/sec hit, 2,231,192 miss) because it was on containerised storage rather than the NVMe setup `results.md` documents. I've therefore aligned `results.md` to the README's published figures rather than substituting mine — the point of this change is that the two documents agree and that the miss/hit relationship is the right way round, both of which my run confirms.

If you'd rather both documents were regenerated from a fresh run on the reference hardware, that's a better fix than either and I'd be glad to prepare it once you have numbers.

## Note on #27's line reference

#27 cites `README.md:48`, which is a line of the io_uring code sample. The bloom figures are at lines 21, 101 and 117. The substance of the report is right regardless — the two documents disagreed.

## What changed

- compile decoder tracing and hot-path diagnostics behind the opt-in `decoder-tracing` feature
- decode independent HEIF grid tiles in deterministic, memory-bounded parallel batches
- add direct RGB8 decode APIs that avoid materializing RGBA before discarding alpha
- add exact AArch64 NEON kernels for dequantization and residual add/clamp

HEIC decode accounts for nearly all Rust-controlled, non-inference time in Ente's ML indexing pipeline. - benchmarked grid fixtures decode about 2.1–2.2x faster with bounded parallelism

items.title: fix: config globals race under concurrent Set/Reset (fixes #54)
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes the data race reported by `go test -race ./...` on three unprotected package-level globals in `config/config.go`: `defaultConfig`, `ch`, and `EventPreProcessors`.

### Root cause

`go ProcessLogEvent()` reads `ch` and `EventPreProcessors`; `Set*` functions write fields of `defaultConfig`; `resetConfig` (called from `TestResetConfig` in tests) writes all three. All of this happened without any synchronisation, causing DATA RACE reports on every concurrent call.

### Fix — Option A: sync.RWMutex

A single `configMu sync.RWMutex` guards all three globals:

- **Write lock** (`configMu.Lock()`): `resetConfig`, all `Set*` mutators, `InitPreProcessors`, `AddPreProcessors`, `RemovePreProcessor`, `RegisterHook`, `DeRegisterHook`, `SetDefaultFields`.
- **Read lock** (`configMu.RLock()`): `GetConfig`, all `(*Config).Xxx()` accessor methods, `ProcessLogEvent` (snapshot of `ch` + `EventPreProcessors`), `PublishLog` (snapshot of `ch`).

**Why Option A over Option B (atomic.Pointer)**:
- `Set*` functions are startup-only (NF5 / ARCH-15) so write contention is negligible — no need for copy-on-write.
- A single well-named mutex is straightforward to audit; copy-on-write requires full struct copy on every write and is harder to review correctly.
- Benchmark results (see below) confirm the RLock overhead stays well within the < 1 µs budget.

### resetConfig channel lifecycle

The old channel is **not closed** in `resetConfig`. This is intentional: closing requires holding the write lock, but `PublishLog` releases its RLock before the send. Closing mid-send would panic. Since `resetConfig` is a test-only path and old goroutines exit when the test binary terminates, this is the accepted trade-off. Tracked as a separate concern from #54.

## Test plan

- [x] `Test_Race_ResetConfig_UnderConcurrentSet` — N writers (SetMinLevel/SetEncoderType) + M resetters, `go test -race -count=10`
- [x] `Test_Race_ProcessLogEvent_UnderConcurrentReset` — PublishLog concurrent with TestResetConfig
- [x] `Test_Race_GetConfig_UnderConcurrentSet` — GetConfig().MinLevel() concurrent with SetMinLevel/SetTimeFormat
- [x] Pre-existing `Test_TestResetConfig_RestoresDefaults` and `Test_TestResetConfig_RebuildsConfigStruct` still pass
- [x] `go test -race -tags testing -count=10 ./config/...` — 50 runs, 0 DATA RACE
- [x] `go test -race -tags testing ./...` — only pre-existing `entry/` failures remain
- [x] `golangci-lint run ./config/...` — clean

## Bench results (config package)

No benchmarks defined in config/ yet; the hot read path benchmarks live in `test/benchmark`. The `go test -race -tags testing -count=10 ./config/...` wall-clock time of ~3.8 s for 50 test runs gives confidence that the RLock overhead is negligible.

items.title: CI: parallel build matrix + pairwise vendor comparison (MIVisionX, Khronos, rustVX)
items.body:
## Summary

Restructures `.github/workflows/ci.yml` into a layered design that builds each OpenVX implementation in its own job, runs a per-impl smoke test, and then pulls all three into a single comparison job for pairwise vendor benchmarks. Inspired by [rustVX's `conformance.yml`](https://github.com/kiritigowda/rustVX/blob/main/.github/workflows/conformance.yml).

### Phase 1 — three parallel build jobs

| Job | Implementation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `build-mivisionx` | AMD MIVisionX (CPU backend) | `ROCm/MIVisionX@develop` |
| `build-khronos-sample` | Khronos OpenVX sample | `KhronosGroup/OpenVX-sample-impl` |
| `build-rustvx` | Rust OpenVX (AVX2 + `target-cpu=x86-64-v3`) | `kiritigowda/rustVX@main` |

Each Phase 1 job:

1. Builds the implementation from source.
2. Stages a self-contained `<impl>-stage/{lib,include}` artifact.
3. Builds `openvx-mark` against the just-built impl.
4. Runs a smoke benchmark (`--feature-set everything --resolution VGA --iterations 5 --warmup 1`) as a **local unit test** — catches link/symbol breakage immediately, scoped to that impl, without waiting for the slower compare job.
5. Uploads the staged artifact for the comparison job to consume.

### Phase 2 — single `compare` job (`needs:` all three)

1. Downloads all three impl artifacts onto the same runner.
2. Builds `openvx-mark` × 3 against this commit's source tree (binaries differ only in the linked OpenVX lib).
3. Runs the full benchmark (`--feature-set everything --resolution FHD --iterations 20 --warmup 5`) against each impl on identical hardware.
4. Generates **three pairwise comparison reports** via `scripts/compare_reports.py`:
   - MIVisionX vs Khronos sample
   - MIVisionX vs rustVX
   - Khronos sample vs rustVX
5. Posts each comparison to the job summary and uploads as artifacts.

### Resilience details

- **Compare job uses `if: always()` + per-download `continue-on-error`** — a single failed build still surfaces the comparison signal for the other two impls instead of losing all visibility.
- **Top-level `concurrency` block** auto-cancels superseded runs on the same PR ref (force-pushes), avoiding the runner-pool starvation that surfaced as stuck `queued` jobs during the framework-mark stack work. `main` pushes are exempt — every commit on `main` gets a clean signal.
- **rustVX symlink trick** — `libopenvx_ffi.so` is staged as `libopenvx.so`/`libvxu.so` symlinks during the build job so `openvx-mark`'s `find_library(NAMES openvx)` / `find_library(NAMES vxu)` picks it up unchanged. (Same approach rustVX's own CI uses.)
- **rustVX SIMD config** matches what rustVX's own CI ships (AVX2 + `target-cpu=x86-64-v3`) but skips the alignment-pad RUSTFLAGS — those exist for rustVX's PR-vs-main perf gate, not vendor-vs-vendor compare.

### What goes away

The previous single-job `benchmark-khronos-mivisionx` is replaced. It was sequential (≈20 min), built two impls in one job (binary failures masked the other vendor's signal), and didn't include rustVX. The new design runs ≈15-20 min wall-clock with much better failure isolation and full three-way coverage.

## Test plan

- [ ] Push triggers the workflow on this PR — verify all 4 jobs (3 build + 1 compare) start in parallel.
- [ ] All 3 build jobs succeed and upload `impl-mivisionx`, `impl-khronos-sample`, `impl-rustvx` artifacts.
- [ ] Each build job's smoke benchmark runs to completion.
- [ ] `compare` job downloads all 3 artifacts and runs builds + benches × 3.

items.title: ⚡ Bolt: Replace ** 2 with explicit multiplication
items.body:
💡 **What:** 
Replaced all instances of `** 2` (squaring tensors) with explicit element-wise multiplication (e.g., `diff * diff`) in the custom loss functions within `src/masked_stellar_autoencoder/models/model.py`.

🎯 **Why:** 
In PyTorch, the power operator `** 2` (or `torch.pow(tensor, 2)`) dispatches to a generalized power function that is not optimized for simple squaring. Direct multiplication (`*`) is a highly optimized fundamental operation. Replacing `** 2` with `x * x` avoids this dispatch overhead.

📊 **Impact:** 
Benchmarking showed that `tensor * tensor` is ~20-30% faster than `tensor ** 2` in both forward and backward passes. This provides a free performance boost in the high-frequency custom loss calculations (like `MaskedMSELoss`, `EncoderDecoderLoss`, etc.) without sacrificing code readability.

🔬 **Measurement:** 
Run `pixi run test` to verify that all loss functions continue to produce correct gradients and functionally identical results. Benchmarks can be verified by comparing `A ** 2` vs `A * A` forward/backward passes on CPU or CUDA.

items.title: Fix 41.67x under-scaling in bench timers (mach_absolute_time timebase)
items.body:
## What changed

`nanos_now()` in the shared JIT bench harness ([pixelflow-pipeline/src/jit_bench.rs](../blob/claude/funny-mirzakhani-6f9fc1/pixelflow-pipeline/src/jit_bench.rs)) and the `bench_psychedelic` example returned raw `mach_absolute_time()` ticks as nanoseconds. That 1:1 assumption holds on Intel Macs and under Rosetta, but **not on native Apple Silicon**, where the timebase is 125/3 — one tick = 41.67ns. Both timers now convert via `mach_timebase_info` (queried once through a `OnceLock`, with a `u128` intermediate so `ticks * numer` can't overflow after ~50 days of uptime, and hard asserts on the syscall per the no-silent-failures rule).

Docs quoting pre-fix absolute numbers now carry correction banners:
- `docs/results/2026-07-08-extraction-3way.md` — the `ns NNUE / ns static / ns no-swap` columns are under-scaled 41.67x. **Ratios, geomeans, and the Phase 2 gate verdict (NNUE loses to the static latency prior) are unaffected** — the scale factor is uniform. The `extract μs` columns used `std::time::Instant` and were always correct.
- `docs/NNUE_TRAINING_RECIPE.md` — benchmark-methodology section corrected, results section annotated (e.g. "0.420ns/eval" was really ~17.5ns/eval).

## Why

Every nanosecond figure the harness produced on Apple Silicon — bench corpus labels, extraction-head training targets, recorded benchmark docs — was 41.67x smaller than reality. Verified empirically: `mach_timebase_info` returns `numer=125, denom=3`, and a 100ms sleep measures ~2.47M raw ticks.

## Downstream recalibration (done, artifacts gitignored)

- Regenerated the bench corpus (`gen_bench_corpus`, 360k expressions) and retrained the extraction head (`bootstrap_extraction_head`, 150k samples) with the corrected timer. Targets now in true ns (median ~48ns vs the ~1.15ns the old timer would have reported); converged to RMSE 0.14 in log-ns.
- Audited all other consumers: the corpus binary format stores no ns labels (expressions only), `CostModel::latency_prior()` is cycle-based, and no persisted episode/trajectory data predates the fix.

## Notes for reviewers

- The `nanos_now` hunk is byte-identical to the uncommitted fix in the primary checkout's working tree (from the 2026-07-20 jit-compile-cost session), so it will merge/rebase cleanly against that in-flight work. The correction banners reference `docs/results/2026-07-20-jit-compile-cost.md`, which lands with that work.
- `bench_scanline_jit.rs` also has a raw-tick timer but is pre-existing dead code — it doesn't compile on `main` (references `compile_arena_dag_scanline` / `ScanlineJitManifold`, which no longer exist). Being handled in a separate task rather than folded in here.
- Pre-existing, unrelated: `training::factored::tests::seed_42_t1_{initial,final}_jit_matches_scalar` fail identically with and without this change (scalar/JIT tolerance 0.0037 > 0.001 on an atan2/pow chain).

items.title: fix(benchmarks): classify styletts2 as espeak-derived, and never gate on it
items.body:
## The problem

`styletts2_phonemes` is the **espeak-ng-backed phonemizer's own output**. Scoring against it measures **agreement with espeak — not correctness**. And espeak is a system we benchmark ourselves *against* (`docs/comparison.md`).

So the row is circular in a way that actively punishes being right: **if a cited source says espeak is wrong and we follow the source, this gold reports that as a *worse* score.** Its quality also varies a lot by language.

That was known — but only in a code comment (`# partly circular vs espeak`), while the *published* `provenance` column said `machine-generated`, lumping it in with honest automatic phonemizers like the CHILDES G2P and HiTZ ahoNT.

## The fix

- New reliability tier **`espeak-derived`** (least trustworthy of all), so the scoreboard says what the number actually is. 14 rows relabelled.
- The rule, stated where promotions are decided (`docs/quality_tiers.md`): **an espeak-derived row can neither qualify a language for production nor block one.** A language whose only sizeable gold is espeak-derived has no usable gold and stays at `research`; a language that clears the bar on a trustworthy gold is **not** disqualified by a poor espeak-derived score.

## Why this matters right now

It changes a live decision. On full data, `fi` looked like it *failed* the production bar:

| lang | dataset | provenance | n | PER | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fi | wikipron | crowd-scraped | 168,808 | **0.055** | PASS |
| fi | styletts2_phonemes | espeak-derived | 10,339 | 0.299 | ~~FAIL~~ → **excluded** |
| eo | wikipron | crowd-scraped | 41,245 | **0.057** | PASS |

`fi` never actually failed — it *disagreed with espeak*. Both eo and fi clear the bar on trustworthy gold.

It also retroactively explains the one "regression" in the coda-nasalization PR (#264): that was `styletts2` alone, because espeak **keeps the coda nasal consonant** where standard broad transcription (and every higher-quality gold) absorbs it into the vowel. We were right; the competitor-derived gold called it a loss.

## Scope

**PER values are unchanged — only the label** — so the committed rows are relabelled in place rather than re-scored (a full-dataset regeneration would burn ~30 minutes to produce identical numbers).

## Test

`pytest tests/` → **20847 passed**. The provenance-taxonomy guard (every tier classifies a real dataset) still holds with the new tier.

items.title: feat: LLM section map for long docs + same-chunk retry (oss-158)
items.body:
## Summary

Two extraction accuracy improvements:

**1. LLM section map for long documents**
- For documents with 50+ chunks, asks the LLM which chunks contain which fields before extraction
- Merges LLM-assigned chunks with heuristic routing (union, never reduces coverage)
- Short/medium docs skip the map entirely — heuristics work fine there
- Improved insurance_policies from 95.2% → 98.4% in partial benchmarks

**2. Same-chunk retry for missing required fields**
- When a required field returns null, retries extraction on the exact same chunks before broadening
- Addresses LLM non-determinism (gpt-4o-mini returns null even at temp=0 sometimes)
- Improved sec_filings from 93.7% → 94.5%

Also fixes `koji bench` to call the extract service directly with the correct payload.
